topic.name: Using the Pythagorean Identity in the First Quadrant

question.text: The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta.$
question.explanation:
Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ as follows:

\[ x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta \]

We're given that $x=\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

\[ \cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}. \]

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta &= 1\\[3pt] \sin^2\theta &= 1 - \cos^2\theta\\[3pt] \sin\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \cos^2\theta} \end{align*}

Substituting $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}$ gives

\begin{align*} \sin\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}\right)^2}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{7}{16}}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{9}{16}}\\[5pt] &=\pm\dfrac{3}{4}. \end{align*}

Finally, we select the positive answer since $\sin\theta$ is positive in the first quadrant. So our final answer is $\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{4}.$

example.title: Computing a Trigonometric Ratio Using the Pythagorean Identity

question.text: The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $y$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\dfrac{\sqrt 5}{4},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $\cos\theta$
question.explanation:
Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ as follows:

\[ x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta \]

We're given that $y=\dfrac{\sqrt 5}{4}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

\[ \sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt 5}{4}. \]

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\cos\theta:$

\begin{align*} \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta &= 1\\[3pt] \cos^2\theta &= 1 - \sin^2\theta\\[3pt] \cos\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta} \end{align*}

Substituting $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt 5}{4}$ gives

\begin{align*} \cos\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 5}{4}\right)^2}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{5}{16}}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{11}{16}}\\[5pt] &=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{11}}{4}. \end{align*}

Finally, we select the positive answer since $\cos\theta$ is positive in the first quadrant. So our final answer is $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{11}}{4}.$

example.title: Computing a Trigonometric Ratio Using the Pythagorean Identity

question.text: The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{5},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $\csc\theta.$
question.explanation:
Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ as follows:

\[ x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta \]

We're given that $x=\dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{5}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

\[ \cos\theta =\dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{5}. \]

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta &= 1\\[3pt] \sin^2\theta &= 1 - \cos^2\theta\\[3pt] \sin\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \cos^2\theta} \end{align*}

Substituting $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{5}$ gives

\begin{align*} \sin\theta &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{5}\right)^2}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{15}{25}}\\[5pt] &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{10}{25}}\\[5pt] &=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{10}}{5}. \end{align*}

We select the positive answer since $\sin\theta$ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{10}}{5}.$

Knowing that $\csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta},$ we have

\begin{align*} \csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{10}}{5}\right)} = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{10}}. \end{align*}

Finally, we rationalize the denominator. \begin{align*} \csc\theta &= \dfrac{5}{\sqrt {10}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{\sqrt {10}}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt {10}}{\sqrt {10}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5\sqrt {10}}{10} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\sqrt {10}}{2} \end{align*}
